definition: The time required for half of the radioactive atoms in a sample to undergo nuclear decay.
The splitting of a heavy atomic nucleus into two lighter nuclei, accompanied by the release of neutrons and thermal energy.
A medium (such as light water, heavy water, or graphite) that slows down fast neutrons to increase the likelihood of fission in fissile material.
The state of a nuclear reactor when the number of neutrons produced by fission equals the number lost through absorption and leakage, maintaining a constant power level.
Thermal energy released as a result of radioactive decay of fission products after a reactor has been shut down.
The SI unit of ionizing radiation dose equivalent, measuring the biological effect of radiation absorbed by human tissue.
The ratio of actual electrical energy produced by a power plant over a period of time compared to its theoretical maximum output operating continuously at full nameplate capacity.
The average net present cost of electricity generation for a generating plant over its lifetime per unit of electricity produced.
Nuclear fuel that has been irradiated in a power reactor and is no longer efficient for sustaining a chain reaction.
A safety philosophy incorporating multiple independent, overlapping barriers and redundant safety measures so that failure of one will not jeopardize safety.
